Caucus

/KAW-kuhs/ - the stress falls on KAW · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Caucus means a private meeting of members working toward the same goal.

The councilors who bike to work formed a caucus, comparing notes over coffee ahead of every transportation vote.

Worked Example

Within the two-hundred-member student senate, the arts caucus is only nine people, but they gather the night before each budget session and arrive speaking with one voice.

A caucus is narrower than a committee: nobody appoints it, and it answers to no chair. Members with a shared goal meet privately, settle their differences among themselves, and walk into the full assembly already aligned.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bloc: members who vote together — the alignment itself, where a caucus is the group that meets

faction: a self-interested wing inside a larger body — often disapproving, where caucus is neutral

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

free-for-all: everyone for themselves, nothing coordinated

opposition: the members working against your goal, not with it

Where it sits · how organized and lasting the gathering is — huddle → caucus → party

huddle vs. caucus: A huddle is a moment's private circle — heads together, then everyone breaks apart again; it has no name and no next agenda.

party vs. caucus: A party goes further than a caucus — permanent, public, and organized, with its own rules, funds, and a name on the ballot.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — caucus

Root — caucus: origin unknown — the word arrived whole in colonial Boston

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: caucus surfaced whole in American English, and even the historians shrug. The word first appears in Boston's club politics before the Revolution; one guess traces it to an Algonquian word for 'counselor,' another to a Latin drinking cup passed at meetings, and neither has been proven. What is certain is what it names — allies meeting privately before the public vote.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Caucus has no root family in English — it turned up in 1760s Boston with its paperwork missing, and both popular guesses about its source (an Algonquian word for counselor, a Latin cup) remain guesses. No other English word grew from it.

Strength Check

Word Choice

political / journalistic

Caucus belongs to the vocabulary of assemblies — legislatures, unions, conventions — for members who organize around one shared goal and meet privately before the body votes. Committee is the official, appointed cousin; bloc is how the votes land. If the gathering is open to everyone, it is not a caucus.
